title: Glacial lake outburst floods: what is standing fact
summary: A glacial lake outburst is a flood with no rain in it. Meltwater collects behind a moraine or an ice dam, something displaces it — a rockfall, an avalanche, a thaw — and the dam fails in minutes. The Himalaya holds tens of thousands of these lakes, India monitors a fraction of them, and the warning systems are almost entirely unbuilt.
india_relevance: India has the largest population exposed to glacial lake outburst floods of any country — about 3 million people live both within 50 km of a glacial lake and within 1 km of a potential flood path. The hazard is also inherently transboundary: the Koshi basin is 2.6% of the Himalaya's southern slope and has produced 51.6% of its recorded glacial lake outbursts, and its upper catchments are in Tibet and Nepal. India's own high-risk lakes sit in Himachal, Sikkim, Ladakh, Arunachal, Jammu & Kashmir and Uttarakhand.

figures.label: Glacial lakes mapped across the Hindu Kush Himalaya
figures.note: A 2005 Landsat baseline, not a current count — lakes have grown and formed since, so this understates today's number. India's own basin atlas counts 28,043 lakes above 0.25 ha, but across whole river basins including Pakistani, Chinese and Nepali territory, so it is not a count of lakes in India.

figures.label: Glacial lakes CWC monitors
figures.note: Plus 358 other water bodies, monitored June to October on Sentinel imagery. The portfolio grew from 902 in 2025. Of these, 681 glacial lakes lie inside India: Arunachal 324, Ladakh 179, Jammu & Kashmir 76, Sikkim 72, Himachal 17, Uttarakhand 13.

figures.label: Lakes on India's high-risk list
figures.note: Himachal 48, Sikkim 41, Ladakh 34, Arunachal 32, Jammu & Kashmir 27, Uttarakhand 13. By type, 103 are moraine-dammed. A 2026 parliamentary reply put 56 of them in the highest risk class.

figures.label: Recorded outbursts across High Mountain Asia
figures.note: About 59 of them in India, per the peer-reviewed version of the database. ICIMOD's own caveat: the record is an underestimate, and the apparent rise over time is mainly better observation rather than more events.

figures.label: People exposed worldwide
figures.note: Living BOTH within 50 km of a glacial lake AND within 1 km of a potential flood path — the two conditions together, which is the part most often dropped in quotation. India holds the largest exposed population of any country, about 3 million. India leads on exposure; on the study's danger index, which weights vulnerability, China and Pakistan rank higher.

figures.label: Glacier mass loss, one decade against the last
figures.note: From −0.17 to −0.28 metres water equivalent a year, between 2000–2009 and 2010–2019, with high confidence. Losses are steepest in the eastern Himalaya.

figures.label: Lakes at high or very high risk, now and by 2100
figures.note: Outburst risk across the Third Pole is projected to roughly triple, with the eastern Himalaya — the transboundary basins above Bihar and Bengal — remaining the primary hotspot under every scenario.

figures.label: End-to-end warning systems commissioned in India
figures.note: The government's own position as of 2026, under a ₹150 crore four-state programme approved in July 2024, of which ₹27.73 crore of ₹135 crore had been released by mid-2025. Two automatic weather stations are confirmed installed, in Sikkim. Press accounts describing twenty or more instrumented lakes contradict the government's own answer.

precedents.what: South Lhonak Lake, Sikkim. 14.7 million m³ of frozen moraine collapsed into the lake, raising a wave around 20 m high that breached the dam and released some 50 million m³ of water. It destroyed the 1,200 MW Teesta-III dam at Chungthang and travelled 385 km down the Teesta into Bangladesh, damaging about 25,900 buildings and 31 major bridges. There was no functioning early warning system; what warning reached people came informally from border police upstream.

toll.label: — and other credible counts run to 102; there is no settled figure

precedents.what: Chorabari Lake above Kedarnath, Uttarakhand, overtopped its moraine and drained in five to ten minutes — the second phase of the disaster, after a rainfall-driven debris flow the day before. A genuine lake outburst, though the lake was rain-fed rather than glacier-fed.

toll.label: for the whole June 2013 Uttarakhand floods; the state later put it above 6,000, and no final count exists

precedents.what: Dig Tsho, Nepal. An ice avalanche into the lake overtopped and cut the end moraine; six to ten million m³ drained in about four hours, destroying a nearly-complete hydro plant 11 km downstream and 14 bridges. It struck during a lull in the trekking season.

toll.label: deaths — the figure of twenty or more in circulation is unsourced

precedents.what: Chamoli, Uttarakhand — commonly filed as a glacial lake outburst and not one. About 27 million m³ of rock and glacier ice fell from Ronti Peak and became a debris flow. No lake was involved; the peer-reviewed account was written specifically to correct the early reporting.

not_counted: Lakes below the monitoring threshold. CWC monitors above 10 hectares; the July 2025 Rasuwa flood came from a supraglacial lake in Tibet that had not been noticed at all.

Anything upstream of the border. India has no gauge above the Tibetan frontier on the Brahmaputra system, and Nepal's Bhote Koshi warning system has a lead time of about six minutes because its sensors are all on the Nepali side of a catchment that begins in Tibet.

The distinction between hazard types, in early reporting. Rock-ice avalanches, landslide-dam breaks and true lake outbursts are routinely reported as one another in the first days, and the correction usually arrives months later in a journal.

withheld: 'About 200 glacial lakes in the Hindu Kush Himalaya are dangerous' — the figure appears in an ICIMOD press release but nowhere in the report it is attributed to, and its likely ancestor is an inventory built partly on topographic maps from 1960–1982.
'178 dead at South Lhonak' — contradicted by every readable source; the disputed range runs from 55 dead with 74 missing to about 102.
'India has the highest GLOF danger in the world' — India has the highest exposed population. On the danger index, which weights vulnerability, China and Pakistan rank above it.
'67 Indian glacial lakes have expanded by more than 40%' — absent from the ISRO page it is attributed to. ISRO's published finding is that 130 lakes in India expanded notably since 1984.
'47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal' — the 47 is a three-country figure. Nepal's share is 21, China's 25 and India's 1.

mechanism.trigger: Something displaces the water or weakens the dam: a rockfall or ice avalanche into the lake, a surge wave that overtops the moraine, or thawing permafrost loosening the frozen debris holding it back. The failure is minutes long, and there is no rain in it.
mechanism.conditions: Glaciers retreat and leave meltwater ponded behind loose moraine — rock and ice debris, never engineered. Mass loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya rose 65% between the 2000s and the 2010s, so the lakes are more numerous, larger and younger than the record they are judged against.
mechanism.assessment: Peer-reviewed work projects outburst risk across the Third Pole roughly tripling by 2100, with lakes rated high or very high risk rising from 1,203 to 2,963, and the eastern Himalaya remaining the hotspot under every scenario. ICIMOD's own caveat is that higher hazard has not yet produced a higher rate of floods.
mechanism.human: What turns an outburst into a disaster is what was built in the path. The 2023 Sikkim flood destroyed a 1,200 MW dam and about 25,900 buildings along the Teesta. India has no end-to-end glacial lake warning system commissioned, and Nepal's Bhote Koshi system has roughly six minutes of lead time because its sensors are all below a border the water starts above.

india_watch: Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh on the Koshi and Gandak; Assam and north Bengal on the Brahmaputra and Teesta. The Koshi basin is 2.6% of the Himalaya's southern slope and has produced 51.6% of its recorded glacial lake outbursts.
what_to_watch: Whether an official agency confirms the mechanism. Himalayan disasters are routinely reported as one thing and found months later to be another — Chamoli 2021 was called a glacier burst and was a rock-ice avalanche.
River levels at the Central Water Commission's downstream gauges, and whether any cross a warning or danger mark.
Whether Copernicus Emergency Mapping is activated, which would produce the first authoritative extent maps.
Whether a landslide dam formed in the flood path. A blockage that fills and then fails produces a second flood, often larger than the first.
The casualty figure settling. Early counts in Himalayan disasters move by an order of magnitude over the first week, and the missing are counted differently by different agencies.
